Chapter 6—Deepening Mindfulness: Working with Thoughts and Emotions.
As mindfulness starts to feel like a familiar companion, the next step is to really tune in to the inner world of your own thoughts and emotions. Now, these mental events can be as fleeting as clouds drifting by—or, sometimes, as intense and stubborn as a full-blown storm. They shape your mood and behavior in all sorts of subtle ways. But here’s the thing: the goal isn’t to control or squash them. It’s about meeting them with openness and understanding.
Have you noticed how thoughts just seem to pop up on their own? Sometimes they replay old stories from the past, or jump ahead, worrying about the future. Some of these thoughts are useful, sure. But many just loop endlessly, or end up being harsh and self-critical.
Mindfulness gently reminds us—thoughts aren’t facts. They’re just mental events, not the absolute truth. And when you start observing them as they come and go, you’ll notice they have a lot less power over you.
One of my favorite metaphors is to picture your thoughts like cars driving down a road. Instead of chasing after every car or trying to stop traffic, imagine yourself just sitting by the roadside, quietly watching each one pass by. There’s a kind of freedom in realizing you don’t have to jump in every vehicle—or get stuck in a traffic jam of your own thoughts.
And what about emotions? Sometimes feelings can be so strong, they sweep you off your feet. But mindfulness encourages a gentle curiosity, no matter if the feeling is pleasant, uncomfortable, or somewhere in between. Even just naming what you’re feeling—like “sadness,” “anger,” or “joy”—can make a real difference. It’s a way of saying, “Hey, I see you,” without letting yourself get swept away.
Sometimes, letting yourself feel an emotion fully—without fighting it—can actually bring relief or clarity you didn’t expect.
Now, when tough emotions show up, there are a few mindful strategies that can really help. Let’s walk through them:
First, acknowledge and name the emotion. Just notice what’s there, without judging yourself.
Second, locate where you feel it in your body. Is there tension, warmth, heaviness? Tune in.
Third, allow the emotion to be there. Give it space, instead of pushing it away.
Next, investigate with curiosity. You might gently ask, “What is this feeling trying to tell me?”
And finally, nurture yourself with kindness. Offer yourself the same compassion you’d give a friend in distress.
These steps form what’s called the “RAIN” approach—Recognize, Allow, Investigate, and Nurture. Practicing RAIN can really transform your relationship with thoughts and emotions, making it easier to respond wisely instead of just reacting on autopilot.
Over time, as you deepen your mindfulness, you’ll notice more emotional resilience. It gets easier to ride out life’s storms, knowing that all thoughts and feelings are just visitors—never permanent residents.
